Hi Emily — thanks for the clear list. Below are concise answers and pointers to attached evidence. If helpful, I can expand any section or set up a 30m call on Thursday.

1) Separation of duties
- Key Admins: responsible for key lifecycle operations (create, import, schedule rotation). Admins are distinct staff in our Cryptography Operations team; actions require MFA + role-bound CLI/API tokens.
- Key Operators: runtime-only principals used by the inference runtime; have encrypt/decrypt/sign permissions via scoped service identities. No ability to export raw key material.
- Escrow/Recovery Operators: a small subset of Compliance Engineers who can initiate escrow workflows; operations require approval from two Key Admins (dual-approval) and a recorded justification.

Minimum privileges: we enforce least privilege via RBAC and IAM policies. Admin role cannot perform runtime decrypt operations unless explicitly granted in a limited emergency path.

2) Escrow / BYOK imports
- We support customer BYOK imports. Customers may provide wrapped key material using their own KMS/HSM or upload via an encrypted import package.
- Escrow is customer-controlled: we store escrowed keys encrypted under a customer-managed wrapping key (CMK) when requested and only release per the documented recovery procedure.
- Escrow lifecycle: creation -> encrypted storage (escrow vault) -> dual-admin approval for retrieval -> retrieval event logged and time-limited access -> escrowed material may be deleted on customer request.
- Who can access: Retrieval requires approval from two Redwood roles (one from Cryptography Ops, one from Compliance) and an explicit customer confirmation (email or signed API token).

3) Emergency access / break glass
- Process: a break-glass request is created in our internal ticketing system (link below). It triggers automated notifications, records approvers, and captures the reason.
- Approvals: at least two named approvers; at least one must be from the security leadership bucket.
- Auditability: all actions are logged to our immutable audit log (append-only) with tamper-evident checksums. Logs are retained for 7 years by default (configurable per enterprise contract).

4) Rotation windows
- Root wrapping keys: recommended rotation 12–24 months; we default to 18 months unless customer requires otherwise.
- Per-tenant data keys: recommended rotation 90–180 days, with automated rotation supported.
- Automatic rotation: supported — customers can choose automatic, scheduled, or manual rotation. Rotations are zero-downtime for active sessions via rolling rewraps and KV cache compatibility checks. See attached rotation SOP.

5) HSM attestations and evidence
- Attached: hsm-attestation-2025-12.pdf (model & firmware baselines); our HSM fleet uses modules validated to FIPS 140-2/3 as noted in the attestation.
- Architecture diagram attached: redwood-kms-architecture-diagram.pdf (shows separation of admin planes, escrow vaults, and runtime identities).

Paul — good question. Short answer: Redwood does not retain unwrapped customer key material in plaintext on general-purpose systems. Recovery options are: 

- Re-wrap to a customer-supplied wrapping key (preferred). In this flow, escrowed material is decrypted inside an HSM boundary and immediately re-wrapped under the customer-provided key; plaintext key material remains inside the HSM ephemeral context and is not written to disk.
- Temporary plaintext exposure: only in extremely limited, auditable circumstances (e.g., hardware failure requiring out-of-band recovery) and requires explicit customer authorization plus two Redwood approvers. Even then, access is performed in a secured, isolated recovery environment with recorded video, split-knowledge operators, and additional attestations.

We can add language to the contract stating a preference for re-wrap-only recoveries and requiring customer confirmation for any plaintext exposure scenario.
